text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's German newspapers:
- Doubts about the sustainability of the current Bonn ruling coalition are growing, as the parties involved are seemingly unable to resolve their differences on Germany's budget problems.

- The leader of the Los Angeles-based Church of scientology condemns Germany for using the "methods of a fascist state" following a decision to put the group under a year-long surveillance by anti-extremist watchdogs.
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) are benefitting from the current debate over European monetary union and the Maastricht criteria guiding the project, a pole found.
- Bonn coalition plans new savings round. A hole of around 10 billion marks still needs to be plugged despite latest plans to sell state shares in Deutsche Telekom worth 10 billion marks.
- GEC Alsthom, one of the manufacturers involved in Francde's TGV high-speed train system, is seeking to enter the German Transrapid project linking Berlin to Hamburg.
- German companies should do more to promote personnel policies that create jobs, a senior official at the Federal Labour Office said.

- Finance Minister Theo Waigel sees critical period for coalition. The fate of the current ruling coalition in Bonn could be decided in the coming four weeks, depending on reactions following the presentation of the 1988 draft budget, Waigel told members of his CSU party in Erlangen.
- Bonn will continue to push ahead with preparations for the euro during discussions at the European Union summit in Amsterdam next week, Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said.
- The German federal government is against plans by regional governments to split up the huge Berlin-based BfA federal pensions body from demands and relocate it in across the regions.
